{{Quote|Over the centuries, Sith scribes simplified this system, creating several less complicated scripts from their hieroglyphic predecessor. While some supplemented the hieroglyphic writing to create the High Sith writing style for ecclesiastical uses, others such as the Common Sith script supplanted it in more mundane settings.|"The Written Word," by Dr. [[Milanda Vorgan]]|<ref name="TWW">{{Hyperspace|url=hyperspace/source/writtenword/index.html?page=1|text=The Written Word|int=The Written Word}}</ref>}}
'''Common Sith''' was a writing system that stemmed from early [[hieroglyphics]] utilized by the [[Sith/Legends|Sith]].

==History==
It was developed over the centuries by Sith scribes who wished to create several less complicated scripts from their hieroglyphic predecessor to write [[Sith (language)|their own language]]. While some supplemented the hieroglyphic writing to create a [[High Sith|style for ecclesiastical uses]], others such as the Common Sith script supplanted it in more mundane settings. A related system was the [[Massassi (alphabet)|Massassi alphabet]]. These writing systems followed the expansion of the [[Sith Empire (Pre-Republic)|Sith Empire]], and enjoyed usage on other worlds, such as [[Ziost/Legends|Ziost]], [[Jaguada/Legends|Jaguada]] and [[Tund/Legends|Tund]].<ref name="TWW" />

Following the discovery of King [[Adas]]'s Empire by the [[Dark Jedi/Legends|Dark Jedi]] [[exiles]], Common Sith script was used also to write [[Galactic Basic Standard/Legends|Galactic Basic Standard]]. The scripts continued to follow the Empire's expansion, [[sector/Legends|sector]] after sector, under the leadership of the [[Jen'jidai]]. Even when the Sith scripts didn't replace others, it did influence and left traces in the scripts of [[Arkanian (language)/Legends|Arkanian]], [[Myke (language)|Myke]] and [[Kruskan (language)|Kruskan]].<ref name="TWW" />

The influence touched even the [[Republic Military/Legends|Republic Military]] during the [[Old Sith Wars]], who adopted Common Sith letter designations for a few [[Ordnance/Regional Depot/Legends|Ordnance/Regional Depot]], such as [[Ord Dalet]], the [[Galactic Empire/Legends|Imperial]] [[Bunker Aleph-One]] on [[Storinal]] and by some [[New Republic/Legends|New Republic]] task forces, such as [[Task Force Aleph]].<ref name="TWW" />

Even after the Sith Empires fell and the species disappeared after the [[Cold War (Galactic Republic–Sith Empire)|Cold War]], the Sith language and its script left an impact not only in its former worlds, but also among [[Dark side of the Force/Legends|dark side]] devotees.<ref name="TWW" />

[[Anakin Skywalker/Legends|Darth Vader]] had Common Sith writing on [[Darth Vader's armor/Legends|his armor's]] chest control panel in the final years of his life.<ref name="TWW" /><ref name="ESB">{{Film|V}}</ref><ref name="ROTJ">{{Film|VI}}</ref>

The access code (''aleph lamed zayin shin'') to bypass the [[Security droid/Legends|security droid]] guarding the [[Imperial Palace/Legends|Imperial Palace's]] residential wing in [[16 ABY/Legends|16 ABY]] was in Common Sith.<ref name="Before the Storm">''[[Before the Storm]]''</ref>

==Behind the scenes==
{{Quote|The Sith, as depicted in ''Golden Age of the Sith'' and ''The Fall of the Sith Empire'', appear very Egyptian in style. To reflect that, and also to justify their use of several different scripts, I loosely echoed the history of Egyptian writing. Both start with hieroglyphics; from that, they develop additional scripts, one used primarily for ecclesiastical purposes (Hieratic/High Sith) and another for everyday use (Demotic/Common Sith).|John Hazlett|<ref name="blog">{{Blog|JSarek|8|Endnotes for The Written Word}}</ref>}}
[[File:VaderChestFunctions.png|thumb|Schematic sketch of Vader's chest plate featuring some fictional alien characters.]]
Fan scrutiny of [[Darth Vader's armor/Legends|Darth Vader's armor]] revealed that the writings on his chest plate/control box differ among appearances, not only between ''The Empire Strikes Back'' and ''Return of the Jedi'', but also in various visual guides, prop exhibitions and close up photos. Some versions of the prop feature letters that are superficially similar or related to [[Wikipedia:Paleo-Hebrew alphabet|Paleo-Hebrew]] [[Wikipedia:abjad|abjad]]; compared to actual Hebrew letters, some appear modified or even flipped on Vader's chest plate.<ref name="vaderchest">{{WebCite|url=http://www.erikstormtrooper.com/sithprophecy.htm|text=Erikstormtrooper's Imperial Gallery|archivedate=20200415144246}}</ref>

The letters can also be seen on a [[Speeder bike/Legends|speeder bike]] prop in the [[Star Wars: The Magic of Myth]] exhibition. 

The writing on Vader's chest plate was identified as Common Sith in [[John Hazlett]]'s [[Hyperspace: The Official Star Wars Fan Club|Hyperspace]]-exclusive article ''[[The Written Word]]'' ([[2010]]), connecting the Hebrew-looking writing with appearances of the term [[Wiktionary:aleph|aleph]] (the Hebrew letter '''[[wikipedia:א|א]]''') in the [[Star Wars Legends]]. Hazlett thought it appropriate to make Sith the in-universe analogue for the script.<ref name="blog" />

Hazlett noted that the Sith appearing in ''[[Star_Wars:_Tales_of_the_Jedi_(comic_series)|Tales of the Jedi]]'' were highly [[Wikipedia:Culture of Egypt|Egyptian]] in appearance, and so decided to establish an analogue. He did this by stating that their language had begun as [[Wikipedia:Egyptian hieroglyphs|hieroglyphics]], before giving rise to both an ecclesiastic script like the [[Wikipedia:Hieratic|Hieratic]] system, and a more common script such as the [[Wikipedia:Demotic (Egyptian)|Demotic]] script.<ref name="blog" />

Hazlett made reference to several species who had adapted Sith writing, such as the [[Arkanian/Legends|Arkanians]], whose Sith connections had been established in [[The Essential Guide to Alien Species (real-world book)|''The Essential Guide to Alien Species'']] ([[2001]]); and the [[Myke]], featured in ''[[Jedi vs. Sith]]'', which fans connected to the Sith/Human hybrids due to their physical similarities.<ref name="blog" />

To encompass other in-universe references to Hebrew, Hazlett tied [[Bunker Twenty-two Aleph|Bunker 22-Aleph]], [[Storinal]] from ''[[X-Wing: Wraith Squadron]]'' ([[1998]]) and [[Task Force Aleph]] from ''[[The New Jedi Order: Agents of Chaos II: Jedi Eclipse]]'' ([[2000]]) to the Sith language. To that end, he identified the [[Aleph-class starfighter|''Aleph''-class starfighter]] from ''[[Legacy of the Force: Betrayal]]'' ([[2006]]) as having Sith connections, but since the described fighter looked little like the Aleph character and more like the [[Wikipedia:Syriac alphabet|Syriac]] "'Ālaph," he specified that it was named after a character from the [[Myke (language)|Myke alphabet]].<ref name="blog" />
